title: A rule for bad days
hookLine: the one-breath version of everything: Hillel teaches the whole Torah to a man standing on one foot
tomorrow: why did a tea master shake leaves onto a path just swept?

lines: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.
cards: Some days the alarm doesn't go off, the bus pulls away as you reach the stop, and the meeting goes sideways before lunch. On a day like that, a whole rule of life feels like a joke.
The Talmud tells of a man who wanted things short too. Not Jewish, and thinking of converting, he came to the sage Shammai and said: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot.
Shammai pushed him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand.

teach.b: So the man went to Hillel and asked the same thing. Hillel didn't laugh, and didn't refuse. He gave him one line: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor.
The rest is commentary. Now go and learn. In the Talmud's telling, Hillel accepted him as a convert, and the story is kept to show Hillel's patience.
Notice its two halves. The first is the one-foot version: one sentence that holds everything.

Jewish teachers call a line like that a kelal, a principle the details hang from. In another source, Rabbi Akiva names the verse "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" a great principle of the Torah.
The second half matters just as much: go and learn. The short version doesn't replace the long one. It's the long one, folded small enough to carry.
A bad day asks for the impossible, like learning everything on one foot.

teach.h: THE WHOLE RULE, ON ONE FOOT.
teach.b: A rule for bad days is your Hillel line: one sentence, said in one breath, that still holds the whole rule. Not a lower bar. The same rule, on one foot.
And when the day turns, the commentary is waiting.

how: Hillel's answer to the man on one foot is told in the Talmud (Shabbat 31a), where it shows his patience. On a personal rule, a bad-day version is one sentence that holds the whole, said in one breath.

games.q: what does “a rule for bad days” mean?
o: a lighter rule that drops the hard parts for good
a one-sentence rule that holds the whole, for hard days
a pause on all practice until life calms down again

games.q: on one foot: tap the pairs.
p: pushed him off with a builder's stick
what is hateful to you, don't do
a principle the details hang from

s: asked to teach the Torah on one foot, Hillel refused
Shammai pushed the man away; Hillel answered with one line.
Hillel ended with: the rest is commentary; go and learn
the one line wasn't the end. go and learn.
a short rule for bad days lowers the standard
Hillel's line was the whole Torah folded small, not a smaller Torah.

games.q: your little brother, swamped before exams, says his study plan is pointless if he can't do all of it tonight. by Hillel's way, what helps?
o: one line that holds the whole plan for tonight; the rest waits for tomorrow.
send him off until he's ready to take the full plan seriously.
tell him the short version is all he'll ever really need.
games.why: Hillel gave one line, then said go and learn. the short form holds the whole, and the long form is still waiting.

practice: Find one sentence that holds your whole rule, short enough to say on a single breath. Breathe in, and on the way out say it out loud, once. Then let the rest of the sit be the commentary: quiet, unhurried, nothing to add.

wordCard.voice: A rule for bad days: one sentence that holds the whole rule, said in one breath. Hillel's way: the whole thing, on one foot.

orig.note: Aramaic, from the Talmud: go and learn, Hillel's last words to the man on one foot.

carryVoice: For the hard days: the one-breath rule, and the rest is commentary, waiting. Day 1699, on one foot.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (the man who asked to learn the Torah on one foot; Shammai's builder's cubit; Hillel: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; the rest is commentary; go and learn)
